eras/carolingian-schism/name: The Carolingians to the Great Schism
eras/carolingian-schism/summary: Charlemagne's coronation by Pope Leo III (800) created a Western empire allied to the papacy, sponsoring liturgical reform, monastic schools and theological debates over predestination and the Eucharist. Byzantium ended iconoclasm for good (843) and launched missions to the Slavs through Cyril and Methodius, while Bulgaria, Serbia and Kievan Rus' (988) embraced Byzantine Christianity. Tensions between Rome and Constantinople grew over the Filioque, papal claims and jurisdiction, flaring in the Photian Schism and culminating in the mutual excommunications of 1054. Monastic reform movements like Cluny (910) revived Western religious life.
eras/carolingian-schism/keyThemes/1: Missions to the Slavs and Scandinavia
eras/carolingian-schism/globalNotes/0/te: Prince Vladimir of Kiev was baptised and led the mass baptism of Kiev's population in 988, tying the East Slavs to Byzantine Orthodoxy and Church Slavonic liturgy.
eras/carolingian-schism/globalNotes/1/te: Disciples of Cyril and Methodius, expelled from Moravia, found refuge in Bulgaria, where the Ohrid and Preslav schools (Clement and Naum of Ohrid) developed Slavonic literature and the Cyrillic script.
eras/carolingian-schism/globalNotes/2/te: The Tang emperor Wuzong's suppression of foreign religions (845) devastated Buddhism and effectively extinguished the Church of the East in China proper for several centuries.
eras/carolingian-schism/globalNotes/3/te: The Church of the East established metropolitans in Merv, Samarkand and beyond; c. 1007 the Keraite Turks of Mongolia reportedly converted, as recorded by the Syriac chronicler Bar Hebraeus.
eras/carolingian-schism/globalNotes/4/te: Christian Nubia (Makuria) flourished, with cathedrals at Faras and Old Dongola decorated with distinctive frescoes, while Ethiopia endured a period of political decline after Aksum.
eras/carolingian-schism/globalNotes/5/te: Copts served prominently in Fatimid administration, but the caliph al-Hakim's persecution (c. 1009–1013) destroyed many churches, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
eras/carolingian-schism/globalNotes/6/te: Copper-plate grants of c. 849 (the Tharisapalli plates) record privileges given by a Kerala ruler to the Christian community of Quilon, linked to the Church of the East.
eras/high-middle-ages/summary: The Gregorian Reform asserted papal independence from secular rulers, leading to the Investiture Controversy and a papacy that reached its height under Innocent III, whose Fourth Lateran Council (1215) defined transubstantiation and required annual confession. The Crusades (from 1096) and the Latin sack of Constantinople (1204) deepened the East–West breach. New religious orders—Cistercians, Franciscans and Dominicans—and the rise of universities produced scholastic theology from Anselm to Thomas Aquinas. Dissenting movements such as the Waldensians and Cathars were met with preaching, crusade and inquisition.
eras/high-middle-ages/keyThemes/1: Crusades and the sack of Constantinople
eras/high-middle-ages/globalNotes/0/text: King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty (c. 1181–1221) commissioned the rock-hewn churches at Roha (Lalibela) as a 'New Jerusalem'; the Solomonic dynasty took power in 1270, fostering a revival of Ge'ez literature.
eras/high-middle-ages/globalNotes/1/text: Many Mongol royal women and some commanders were Church of the East Christians; Rabban Sauma, a Uyghur or Öngüt monk born near Beijing, travelled to Rome and Paris as an envoy of the Ilkhanate (1287–1288).
eras/high-middle-ages/globalNotes/2/text: Yahballaha III, an Öngüt from China, was elected catholicos of the Church of the East (1281), symbolising its vast reach just before Ilkhanid conversion to Islam (1295) brought renewed persecution.
eras/high-middle-ages/globalNotes/3/text: Under the Yuan (Mongol) dynasty, Church of the East communities revived in China, and the Franciscan John of Montecorvino arrived in Khanbaliq (Beijing) in 1294, later becoming its first Latin archbishop.
eras/high-middle-ages/globalNotes/4/text: The Mongol conquest of Rus' (1237–1240) placed the Russian church under the Golden Horde, which generally exempted clergy from tribute; Alexander Nevsky resisted Western crusading pressure from Swedes and Teutonic Knights.
eras/high-middle-ages/globalNotes/5/text: Armenian Cilicia allied with the crusaders and engaged in union talks with Rome, while Georgia under Queen Tamar (1184–1213) reached a golden age of Orthodox culture.
eras/high-middle-ages/globalNotes/6/text: Coptic scholarship flowered in Arabic, notably the encyclopaedic works of the Awlad al-Assal brothers in the thirteenth century.
eras/late-medieval/summary: The papacy's residence at Avignon (1309–1377) and the Western Schism (1378–1417), with two and then three rival popes, damaged papal prestige and spurred the conciliar movement, which ended the schism at Constance (1414–1418). Plague, war and social upheaval fostered intense lay devotion, mysticism and the Devotio Moderna, alongside critics such as Wycliffe and Hus whose followers anticipated later reformations. In the East, Hesychasm was affirmed under Gregory Palamas, a brief reunion was proclaimed at Florence (1439) but rejected, and Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Spanish and Portuguese voyages at the century's end opened the way to global Catholic missions.
eras/late-medieval/keyThemes/0: Avignon, the Western Schism and conciliarism
eras/late-medieval/keyThemes/3: Wycliffe, Hus and calls for reform
eras/late-medieval/keyThemes/4: Hesychasm and the fall of Constantinople
eras/late-medieval/globalNotes/0/text: Timur's campaigns (1370s–1405) and the conversion of Mongol successor states to Islam destroyed most Church of the East communities in Central Asia and Persia, leaving survivors chiefly in the mountains of Kurdistan and in India.
eras/late-medieval/globalNotes/1/text: Emperor Zara Yaqob (1434–1468) reformed the Ethiopian church, enforced Sabbath observance alongside Sunday and sent delegates to the Council of Florence; the monastic leader Ewostatewos had earlier championed the Sabbath. Christian Nubia faded after the fall of Dongola, with Makuria disappearing by the late fifteenth century.
eras/late-medieval/globalNotes/2/text: Sergius of Radonezh (d. 1392) founded the Holy Trinity monastery and inspired a monastic revival; Moscow rejected the Union of Florence, its church became effectively autocephalous in 1448, and after 1453 some spoke of Moscow as a successor to Byzantium.
eras/late-medieval/globalNotes/3/text: Portuguese navigators reached the Kingdom of Kongo (1483); King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised as João I in 1491, beginning a Kongolese Catholic tradition led by African rulers.
eras/late-medieval/globalNotes/4/text: Columbus' 1492 voyage opened the Americas to Spanish conquest; papal bulls of 1493 and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided mission and colonial rights between Spain and Portugal.
eras/late-medieval/globalNotes/5/text: Under Mamluk rule the Coptic church suffered recurrent discriminatory decrees and riots in the fourteenth century, accelerating conversion to Islam and the decline of Coptic as a spoken language.
eras/late-medieval/globalNotes/6/text: Gregory Palamas' defence of the hesychast monks of Mount Athos and the distinction between God's essence and energies were endorsed by councils in Constantinople (1341–1351).
eras/reformations/summary: Martin Luther's protest against indulgences (1517) grew into a reformation of doctrine centred on justification by faith and the authority of Scripture, followed by Reformed (Zwingli, Calvin), Anabaptist and Anglican movements, each with distinct theologies and church orders. The Catholic Church answered with the Council of Trent (1545–1563), new orders such as the Jesuits, and renewed spirituality. Confessional conflict produced wars of religion culminating in the Thirty Years' War, ended by the Peace of Westphalia (1648). At the same time Catholic missions spread Christianity across the Americas, Africa and Asia on an unprecedented scale.
eras/reformations/keyThemes/0: Justification by faith and sola scriptura
eras/reformations/keyThemes/1: Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist and Anglican reformations
eras/reformations/keyThemes/2: Catholic Reform and the Council of Trent
eras/reformations/globalNotes/0/text: The Spanish conquest of Mexico (1519–1521) and Peru brought mass baptisms and mendicant missions; Bartolomé de las Casas condemned abuses of Indigenous peoples, informing the Valladolid debate (1550–1551), and the Guadalupe devotion took root in Mexico.
eras/reformations/globalNotes/1/text: Francis Xavier arrived in Japan in 1549; by 1600 Japan had perhaps 300,000 Christians, but persecution from 1614 forced 'hidden Christians' underground. Matteo Ricci reached Beijing in 1601, adapting Christianity to Confucian culture.
eras/reformations/globalNotes/2/text: Portuguese Goa became a mission centre; the Synod of Diamper (1599) imposed Latin practices on the St Thomas Christians, a grievance that erupted in the Coonan Cross Oath (1653) just after this era.
eras/reformations/globalNotes/3/text: Portuguese troops helped Ethiopia repel the Adal invasion of Ahmad Gragn (1529–1543); later Jesuit influence led Emperor Susenyos to declare Catholicism (1622), provoking civil war and his abdication, after which Fasilides expelled the Jesuits (1633).
eras/reformations/globalNotes/4/text: The Moscow Patriarchate was established in 1589, and the Union of Brest (1596) brought part of the Ruthenian Orthodox church into communion with Rome as the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church.
eras/reformations/globalNotes/5/text: King Afonso I of Kongo (r. c. 1509–1542) promoted Catholicism, and his son Henrique was consecrated a bishop in 1518, the first sub-Saharan African bishop of the Latin church.
eras/reformations/globalNotes/6/text: Spanish Augustinians, Franciscans and Dominicans evangelised the Philippines after 1565, making it the first predominantly Christian society in Asia.
eras/confessional-pietism/summary: After Westphalia, Protestant churches consolidated their doctrine in detailed scholastic systems, while Catholicism experienced baroque devotion alongside the Jansenist controversy. Reacting against arid orthodoxy, Pietism under Spener and Francke stressed new birth, small groups and practical holiness, and radical movements such as the Quakers emphasised the inner light. The Enlightenment's rise brought deism, biblical criticism and growing calls for toleration. In Russia, Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms caused the Old Believer schism, and Peter the Great replaced the patriarchate with a state-controlled Holy Synod.
eras/confessional-pietism/keyThemes/1: Pietism and the religion of the heart
eras/confessional-pietism/keyThemes/4: Old Believers and Peter the Great's church reform
eras/confessional-pietism/globalNotes/0/: Patriarch Nikon's reforms (1650s) aligning Russian rites with Greek usage were resisted by the Old Believers led by Archpriest Avvakum (burned 1682); Peter the Great abolished the patriarchate and created the Holy Synod (1721).
eras/confessional-pietism/globalNotes/1/: Emperor Kangxi's edict of toleration (1692) favoured Jesuit missions, but the Chinese Rites controversy—papal rulings of 1704 and 1715 forbidding Confucian rites—led Kangxi to restrict Christianity.
eras/confessional-pietism/globalNotes/2/: The Coonan Cross Oath (1653) split the St Thomas Christians; one party later entered communion with the Syriac Orthodox Church (from 1665). Lutheran Pietist missionaries Ziegenbalg and Plütschau arrived at Tranquebar (1706) and translated the New Testament into Tamil (1714).
eras/confessional-pietism/globalNotes/3/: In Kongo, Beatriz Kimpa Vita led the Antonian movement (1704–1706), an Africanised Catholic prophetic movement; she was burned as a heretic, an early forerunner of African Initiated Churches.
eras/confessional-pietism/globalNotes/4/: Jesuit 'reductions' among the Guaraní in Paraguay reached their peak, sheltering tens of thousands from slave raiders; Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz wrote theology and poetry in Mexico.
eras/confessional-pietism/globalNotes/5/: Divisions within the Church of the East produced rival patriarchal lines, one of which entered union with Rome, the origin of the Chaldean Catholic Church (formalised 1830).
